def: The value placed on property when it last changed ownership (or was newly built); grows at most 2% per year thereafter.
Base year value after annual 2% inflation factors.
A transfer that resets assessment to current market value unless an exclusion (like Prop 19) applies.
Parent-child exclusion protects taxable value only up to factored base year value + ~$1M (biennially adjusted); anything above is added to taxable value.
Inherited assets generally take a new tax basis equal to fair market value at death, wiping out pre-death gain for the heir.
Up to $250,000/$500,000 of gain on a principal residence can be excluded if the 2-of-5-year ownership and use tests are met.
Federal estate tax return; also the vehicle for portability (DSUE) even when no tax is due.
A deceased spouse's unused exclusion transferred to the surviving spouse by filing a timely Form 706.
California's 1% tax on taxable income above $1,000,000 (Form 540 line 62; formerly Mental Health Services Act).
3.8% federal net investment income tax on investment income once MAGI exceeds $200,000 (single) / $250,000 (joint).
Tax due when real property changes hands — Santa Clara County charges 0.11%; San Francisco's tiered tax reaches 6%.
A flat per-parcel charge (like SF Prop H) billed with property tax; not ad valorem.
Special assessments for services/bonds that add to the property tax bill outside the 1% base.
The risk that sale proceeds must be redeployed into markets at unfavorable prices — the mirror image of selling too early.
The implicit rental value of living in a home you own — the benefit you forgo when you rent it out instead.
CPUC tariff crediting new solar exports at avoided cost rather than retail rate (effective 2023-04-15).
SF rule allowing market rent reset when a tenant voluntarily vacates a covered unit.
An extreme, hard-to-predict market event (1929, 2008) that invalidates baseline projections.
Investing sale proceeds in tranches over months/years instead of all at once to reduce single-date timing risk.
Liquid assets ÷ total net worth — how much of the estate can be turned to cash quickly.
